attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his roundup. The embedded OpenAI post is used only to identify which model the 80% cut applied to.

semantics.note: The statement asserts a cause outright (competition drove the cut), so causal is the right kind. Reading the 80% as the Luna cut matches the announcement he embedded.

contract.note: Treating competition as a material cause rather than the only cause is fair to his words. Limiting the 80% to Luna is the ordinary reading given the embedded post. The contract correctly asks for direct evidence of motive.

evidence.note: Confirms the 80% Luna cut effective July 30. Its line that competition 'likely' played a role is the outlet's own inference, so it does not establish the cause.
OpenAI's announcement confirms the cut and credits efficiency gains. As a company statement about itself, it neither proves nor rules out competitive pressure.

reviews.rationale: The 80% Luna price cut is verified. The causal part is not settled. No direct statement, decision record or well-sourced report shows competition was a material driver. The Decoder only infers it, and OpenAI gives efficiency as its explanation. The contract requires both parts, so the claim is unresolved.

attribution.note: Marcus's own description in his roundup. The links to NYT coverage and to an X post are pointers, not a quoted claim.

semantics.note: It reports an event and keeps his words. 'Hubris-fueled' is correctly set aside as his own characterization.

contract.note: Reading 'downfall' as a severe reversal with forced sales, not necessarily dissolution, is a fair ordinary reading. The result depends on that reading, but it is not stretched for or against him.

evidence.note: CNBC, July 30: the fund was forced to sell all its public holdings after steep losses while its brokers raised cash to meet margin requirements.
Reports roughly 4x leverage, margin calls and the sale of the public book to Citadel. This is an estimate, not an audited figure.

The fund kept private stakes, mainly in Anthropic. CNBC also cites reports of up to 400% leverage and calls it a near-collapse. This rules out reading the downfall as total dissolution, but is consistent with a severe reversal.

reviews.rationale: Contemporaneous reporting shows heavy losses, margin calls and the forced sale of the fund's entire public portfolio, with leverage reported at about 4x. That meets the contract's reading of a severe, highly leveraged reversal. The fund still holds private stakes, so it did not cease to exist, but the contract does not require that. 'Hubris' was not tested.

attribution.note: Marcus himself states that MIT Technology Review published this report. The claim being scored is that attribution, not the article's own findings.

semantics.note: Faithful to his words. 'Disturbing' is kept as his own evaluation.

contract.note: Asking for a dated MIT Technology Review jailbreaking article in the July 30–31 window is a fair plain reading. Treating 'new' as describing the reporting is reasonable.

evidence.note: MIT Technology Review article dated July 30, 2026 reporting chain-of-thought forgery jailbreaks against OpenAI and other models. That the technique was discovered earlier does not change the publication date.

reviews.rationale: MIT Technology Review published an article on July 30, 2026 reporting jailbreak attacks on LLMs. This matches the claimed attribution, the time window and the subject.
